analysis.one_liner: Lets state and local governments end federal court oversight agreements after four years or a change in leadership.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee hearing or vote and died in the Senate Judiciary Committee at the end of the 110th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal consent decrees are court orders that state or local governments agree to when they are found to be violating federal law — for example, orders fixing prison conditions, jail overcrowding, or police practices. This bill would let any state or local government ask a court to modify or end such a decree after four years, or as soon as the top elected official who agreed to it left office. It would shift the burden of proof onto the people who won the decree, who would have to prove continued court oversight was necessary or see it terminated. The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee and never went anywhere.
analysis.who_benefits: State and local governments and the elected officials who run them — especially those seeking to escape long-running court supervision over prisons, jails, police departments, or social service agencies. Once a new governor, mayor, or other top official takes office, that administration could move to end decrees its predecessor agreed to, and the court would have to end them unless the original plaintiffs could prove continued supervision was necessary to stop a federal violation.

how_it_helps.text: Lets state and local governments move to modify or terminate a consent decree after the earlier of four years or the end of the term of the highest elected official who was a party to it.

Shifts the burden of proof to the party that originally filed the lawsuit, which must prove that keeping the decree is necessary to prevent a violation of federal law addressed in the original decree; if it fails, the court must terminate the decree.
Requires courts to move quickly — a scheduling order within 30 days and a final ruling within 180 days, with the power to suspend the decree's relief if opponents seek delays.

Explicitly excludes school desegregation orders and cases filed by the United States, and requires the Attorney General to report annually to Congress on federal consent decrees four or more years old.

analysis.who_pays: The people consent decrees protect — prisoners and jail inmates, psychiatric patients, children in state custody, and residents of cities under court-ordered police reforms. Once a decree is terminated, they would have to file a new lawsuit and win it to get court-ordered fixes back.

drawbacks.text: By placing the burden of proof on the original plaintiffs and requiring termination if they fail to meet it, the bill makes it far harder to keep court-ordered reforms in place once a government moves to end them.

The bill applies retroactively to every existing consent decree, regardless of when it was entered or whether any relief has already been obtained under it, abruptly changing the rules for settlements already negotiated.

An incoming administration could end a decree fixing prison conditions, police misconduct, or foster care without showing those problems are fixed — leaving the affected residents to start new litigation from scratch.

Supporters' good-faith argument is that decrees can persist for decades and bind new administrations to their predecessors' policy choices; the bill's counterweight is that it does so by making termination nearly automatic, with no showing required that the underlying violation has been remedied.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addresses a real concern — some consent decrees run for decades and bind future administrations — but its remedy is lopsided. It does not require a departing government to show that the problems the court found are fixed; it requires the people who won the decree to prove, on a fast 180-day clock, that continued supervision is necessary, and terminates the decree if they cannot. For vulnerable populations whose court-enforced protections depend on these decrees, the cost would fall directly on them, while the benefit — faster exit from oversight — goes to officeholders and governments.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it, so it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Lamar Alexander introduced the bill on November 1, 2007, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary.
No further action was ever taken — no hearings, no markup, no floor vote — and the bill died in committee at the end of the 110th Congress.
The bill drew 13 cosponsors, 11 Republicans and 2 Democrats (Sens. Pryor and Nelson of Nebraska).

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People and groups protected by federal consent decrees against state and local governments — prisoners, institutionalized patients, and residents under police-reform orders — are better off because the bill never advanced, since their court-enforced protections were not cut back. State and local governments were no worse off, since they simply remained under the existing rules for ending decrees.

industries.industry: State and local governments and elected officeholders
industries.note: The bill would hand governments an easy exit from court-ordered oversight after four years or an election, with the burden of proof reversed against the people who won the decrees. Their gain — freedom from supervision — comes directly at the expense of residents the decrees protect.

industries.industry: Civil rights plaintiffs and the lawyers who represent them
industries.note: The bill would shift the burden of proving a decree is still necessary onto the original plaintiffs and set a 180-day clock, raising their cost of holding governments to court-ordered reforms. Their interest runs alongside the residents they represent.
